rows.title: Cracking differential mount (studs rip out of the frame)
rows.howToFix: If caught early you may only need fresh rubber diff mounting bushings, but the proven bulletproofing fix is a reinforcement kit: weld in a Moss/Sport Car Parts differential-mount repair kit that adds new studs, brackets and (on the front) reinforcing plates that spread the load and stop the crack from returning. The job is done with the diff out — grind out and weld up any existing crack, fit the reinforcing plate over the cross-member, install the new pin/studs, and renew the mount bushings at the same time. Polyurethane diff mount bushings are a common durability upgrade over the soft OEM rubber.
rows.dispositionReason: At least one replacement is conditional on a stated diagnostic result.

rows.title: Crankshaft thrust-washer wear and excessive end float
rows.howToFix: Check end float with a dial indicator (lever the crank fore/aft) at every opportunity and especially after break-in; if it exceeds ~0.010–0.012 in, pull the centre main cap and fit oversize thrust washers to bring float back to 0.006–0.008 in. Restorers bulletproof this during a rebuild by fitting quality thrust washers and, on the best builds, having the bearing holder machined for bronze thrust washers/bushings instead of the original whitemetal. The cheapest insurance is the driving habit the community insists on: put the gearbox in neutral and release the clutch at stoplights instead of sitting with the pedal down.

rows.title: Lucas charging and electrical gremlins (corroded earths, weak alternator)
rows.howToFix: Restorers cure it at the root: fit a quality reproduction wiring harness, then clean and protect every earth point (engine-to-frame and frame-to-body bonding straps added), and clean the brown feed wires and battery terminals. The popular bulletproofing upgrades are converting the points distributor to electronic ignition (Pertronix), and swapping the old 16ACR-style alternator for a modern higher-output internally-regulated alternator so the gauges and any added electric fan have reliable current. Note: with electronic ignition, never crank or run with a plug lead off — it can fry the module.

rows.title: Lucas PI petrol-injection: hot-start failure, blocked injectors, fuel surge
rows.howToFix: Two proven paths. Keep-it-original camp: rebuild the metering unit and injectors, replace worn throttle shafts, fit a modern Bosch high-pressure pump conversion kit (Revington TR) in place of the failure-prone original Lucas pump, and install a tank with the correct anti-surge reservoir to cure cornering starvation. Reliability-first camp: convert to twin Stromberg/SU or Weber carburettors (the US-spec setup) for far easier tuning and dependable starting, accepting a small power trade. Either way, address the anti-surge tank so the car doesn't cut out in corners.

rows.title: Marginal cooling / overheating in traffic and hot weather
rows.howToFix: Bulletproof the system as a package rather than chasing one part: refresh the basics first (verify the thermostat opens, correct belt tension, healthy water pump, full flush) then fit an aluminum cross-flow/high-capacity radiator (Wizard Cooling, US Radiator) sized for the TR6, and add a thermostatically-switched electric cooling fan (e.g. Hayden/Spal ~14 in) which the community reports drops idle temps roughly 6–10°F and removes the parasitic drag of the engine fan. A 13-blade 'tropical' fan is the cheaper interim fix if staying engine-driven. Always confirm ignition timing and mixture, since a lean/retarded TR6 runs hot.

rows.title: Perished rear-suspension bushings causing rear camber/handling vagueness
rows.howToFix: The standard bulletproofing rebuild is polyurethane trailing-arm bushings (SuperPro/Prothane) in place of the worn rubber for a firmly-planted rear without a harsh ride, combined with Goodparts/Richard Good adjustable trailing-arm brackets so rear camber can actually be set correctly instead of living with the factory's excess negative camber. Do it alongside fresh shocks/springs and a full inspection of the trailing-arm mounts, since the same area is the chassis crack/rust hot-spot. Properly set up, owners report flat, predictable cornering and even tyre wear.
